items.name: Modus Tollens
items.summary: Valid conditional inference: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
items.detail: Modus tollens is the contrapositive form. Whenever a conditional 'P → Q' is true, the contrapositive '¬Q → ¬P' is logically equivalent. The LSAT loves to test contrapositive recognition because students who only memorize 'P → Q' miss that the same rule also tells you what happens when Q fails.
examples: If the contract is enforceable, both parties signed. The contract was not signed by both parties. ∴ The contract is not enforceable.

items.name: Modus Ponens
items.summary: Valid conditional inference: if P then Q; P; therefore Q.
items.detail: The simplest valid conditional inference. Distinguish from the *invalid* mirror moves — affirming the consequent (Q ∴ P) and denying the antecedent (¬P ∴ ¬Q) — both classic LR flaw types.
examples: All senior partners have argued before the supreme court. Maria is a senior partner. ∴ Maria has argued before the supreme court.

items.name: Conditional Reasoning
items.summary: Working with 'if/then' statements, their contrapositives, and chains of conditionals.
items.detail: Indicators: 'if', 'only if', 'unless', 'whenever', 'all', 'every', 'no', 'none'. 'Only if' attaches to the *necessary* condition; 'unless' translates to '¬X → Y'. Always diagram conditionals before answering and always check the contrapositive.
examples: Only members may vote → Vote → Member (and ¬Member → ¬Vote).
Unless you submit by Friday, your filing is late → ¬Submit-by-Friday → Late.

items.name: Contrapositive
items.summary: The contrapositive of 'P → Q' is '¬Q → ¬P'; logically equivalent.
items.detail: Contraposition is the workhorse of LR conditional questions. Note: the *converse* (Q → P) and the *inverse* (¬P → ¬Q) are NOT equivalent — confusing them is the affirming-the-consequent / denying-the-antecedent flaw.
examples: P → Q is equivalent to ¬Q → ¬P, but not to Q → P or ¬P → ¬Q.

items.name: Necessary Assumption
items.summary: An unstated premise the argument REQUIRES in order to hold.
items.detail: Use the negation test: negate the candidate; if the argument collapses, it was necessary. Necessary assumptions are minimally helpful — they fill the smallest possible gap, not the most ambitious.
examples: Argument: 'A or B; not A; ∴ B.' Necessary assumption: those were the only options.

items.name: Sufficient Assumption
items.summary: An assumption strong enough to GUARANTEE the conclusion.
items.detail: Sufficient-assumption answers can be much stronger than necessary ones. The trick is to map the gap between premise and conclusion and find the answer that closes it completely.

items.name: Causation vs. Correlation
items.summary: Inferring cause from a mere correlation is a classic LR flaw.
items.detail: When an argument says 'X and Y are correlated, therefore X causes Y', look for: (a) reverse causation (Y → X), (b) common cause (Z → both), (c) coincidence, (d) selection bias. Weaken answers usually surface one of these alternatives.
examples: Breakfast eaters score higher on cognitive tests → eating breakfast causes cognitive performance? Could be sleep, exercise, or socioeconomic confounders.

items.name: Alternative Cause
items.summary: A confounding variable that explains the observed pattern equally well or better.
items.detail: Most LR weaken answers introduce an alternative cause. Strengthen answers usually rule one out.

items.name: Weaken Question
items.summary: Pick the answer that, if true, most undermines the argument.
items.detail: Identify the conclusion, then attack the link between premise and conclusion — typically by surfacing a counter-example, alternative cause, or unmet assumption. Avoid answers that simply contradict a premise (the LSAT treats premises as given).

items.name: Strengthen Question
items.summary: Pick the answer that, if true, most supports the argument.
items.detail: Mirror image of weaken: rule out alternative explanations, supply a missing assumption, or provide additional confirming evidence.

items.name: Flaw in the Reasoning
items.summary: Identify the logical error the argument commits.
items.detail: Common flaws: ad hominem, circular reasoning, equivocation, hasty generalization, sampling bias, appeal to ignorance, false dichotomy, conflating correlation with causation, part-whole conflations, conditional reasoning errors (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent).

items.name: Equivocation
items.summary: Using one word in two different senses across an argument.
items.detail: Tricky because the equivocated term is often subtle ('volume of submissions' vs. 'diversity of viewpoints', or 'theory' as 'guess' vs. 'theory' as 'scientific framework'). Watch for shifts in scope between the premise and conclusion.

items.name: Appeal to Ignorance
items.summary: Treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence (or vice versa).
items.detail: 'No one has shown X is true, therefore X is false' — and its mirror 'No one has shown X is false, therefore X is true.' Both are flawed because lack of evidence settles nothing.

items.name: Parallel Reasoning
items.summary: Match the abstract STRUCTURE of the stimulus, not its subject matter.
items.detail: Diagram the stimulus as variables (P, Q, R…). Then test each answer choice by diagramming it the same way. The correct answer must match the validity status (valid ↔ valid, invalid ↔ same kind of invalid) and the structural shape.

items.name: Universal Instantiation
items.summary: From 'all P are Q' and 'x is P', conclude 'x is Q'. Always valid.
items.detail: The bedrock valid argument form. Distinguish from 'most P are Q' (probabilistic) and 'some P are Q' (existential).

items.name: Main Point Question
items.summary: Identify the central thesis of the passage.
items.detail: The main point summarizes the WHOLE passage, not a single paragraph. Wrong answers are usually too narrow (a single example) or too broad (a vague abstraction).

items.name: Passage Structure
items.summary: Map each paragraph's role: setup, complication, evidence, counter-argument, resolution.
items.detail: Before answering questions, jot a one-line label for each paragraph. Most RC question types (main point, author attitude, role of statement, function of paragraph) become trivial once the structural map is clear.

items.name: Author's Attitude / Tone
items.summary: Identify the author's stance toward the subject — endorsement, skepticism, neutrality, etc.
items.detail: Look for evaluative adjectives, hedge words ('arguably', 'risks'), and rhetorical questions. Hedged language usually means a hedged answer (qualified concern, cautious optimism) is right.

items.name: Tone
items.summary: Closely related to author attitude — measure intensity (mild/strong) and polarity (positive/negative).
items.detail: Eliminate extremes ('uncritical', 'open hostility') unless the passage explicitly supports them.

items.name: Detail Question
items.summary: Ask what the passage explicitly states. Always go back to the text.
items.detail: The right answer is paraphrased directly from a specific sentence; trap answers are inferences (correct, but not stated) or close-but-not-quite restatements.

items.name: Sequencing Game
items.summary: Place items in a strict order (1st through nth) under constraints.
items.detail: Diagram with slots. Render rules as adjacency blocks (F-H), distance constraints, and forbidden positions. Make a hypothetical for any rule that creates few options.

items.name: Rule-Elimination
items.summary: Quickly knock out 'could be the order' answer choices by checking one rule at a time.
items.detail: On orientation questions, scan the answers rule-by-rule rather than building a master diagram. Each rule typically eliminates exactly one answer.

items.name: Must Be True
items.summary: An answer that holds in every case consistent with the given statements.
items.detail: In LG: build the hypothetical, force every implication, then evaluate each answer — if even one valid layout makes the answer false, it doesn't 'must be true'. In LR: the credited inference must follow strictly from the stimulus; watch for quantifier downgrades ('all' → 'most' → 'some') and reversed conditionals in the traps.

items.name: Could Be True EXCEPT
items.summary: Four answers are possible in some valid layout; one is impossible. Pick the impossible.
items.detail: Treat as a 'must be false' question. Construct counter-examples for the four 'could' options; the remaining choice is your answer.

items.name: Main Conclusion
items.summary: Identify the statement the rest of the argument exists to support.
items.detail: The main conclusion is what everything else supports and what supports nothing further. Indicator words help ('therefore', 'thus') but the LSAT loves burying the conclusion first or mid-argument and decorating premises with conclusion-like language. Test a candidate by asking 'does anything in the argument support THIS?' — if yes, keep climbing.
examples: 'Since the statute is ambiguous, and ambiguous statutes are construed against the drafter, the clause should be read narrowly.' Main conclusion: read the clause narrowly.

items.name: Resolve the Paradox
items.summary: Find the fact that lets two apparently conflicting findings both be true.
items.detail: The stimulus reports a surprising discrepancy ('sales rose while ad spending fell'). The credited answer adds information that dissolves the tension without denying either finding. Wrong answers explain only one side, deepen the mystery, or drift out of scope.
examples: Fewer traffic tickets were issued, yet accident rates fell. Resolver: cameras replaced officers and deter violations without issuing tickets.

items.name: Method of Reasoning
items.summary: Describe HOW the argument proceeds, not whether it succeeds.
items.detail: Common techniques: counterexample, analogy, reductio ad absurdum, eliminating alternatives, appealing to a general principle, attacking a premise vs. attacking reasoning. The credited answer describes the move at the right abstraction level; traps describe techniques the argument never uses or misidentify the target of an objection.
examples: 'Opponents claim X; but X implies Y, and Y is absurd; so not-X' — a reductio.

items.name: Principle Application
items.summary: Match a general rule to the concrete case that satisfies all of its conditions.
items.detail: Treat the principle as a conditional with (possibly several) trigger conditions and an exception clause. The conforming case satisfies every trigger and no exception. Traps satisfy most-but-not-all conditions, trip the exception, or run the principle backwards (concluding the trigger from the result).
examples: Principle: a lawyer may withdraw only if withdrawal will not prejudice the client. Case that conforms must show BOTH withdrawal AND no prejudice.

items.name: RC Inference
items.summary: What the passage most strongly supports beyond its explicit statements.
items.detail: Unlike detail questions, the credited answer is not stated — it follows from combining two or three passage claims. It stays modest: hedged language in the passage yields hedged inferences. Traps are real-world plausible but textually unsupported, or turn 'some commentators argue' into the author's own view.
examples: Passage: defenders cite discovery abuse; critics cite access. Supported inference: the parties disagree about which cost matters more — NOT that either side would abolish pleading standards.

items.name: Grouping Game
items.summary: Select or distribute entities into groups under membership rules.
items.detail: Two families: selection (in/out of one group, e.g. 'choose four of seven') and distribution (partition into teams). Diagram membership conditionals ('If J is in, K is out' → J → ¬K) and chain contrapositives. Numeric limits (group sizes) drive most hard inferences.
examples: If J is selected then K is not; if K is not selected then L is. Selecting J forces L.
